articles.title: x402 vs card and ACH for freight: why an agent buyer needs a payment rail built into HTTP
articles.excerpt: Every freight broker already takes money somehow. Shippers pay invoices by ACH, wire, check, or a card on a portal. Those rails work. They moved trillions of dollars of goods long before anyone talked…
articles.body: Every freight broker already takes money somehow. Shippers pay invoices by ACH, wire, check, or a card on a portal. Those rails work. They moved trillions of dollars of goods long before anyone talked about AI agents. So when Nettrux says it is the first 3PL on x402, a fair question from a shipping manager or a CFO is: why add another payment rail at all? The short answer is that the buyer is changing. Card and ACH flows assume a person is somewhere in the loop at the moment of payment: typing a number into a form, clicking a 3-D Secure prompt, uploading a remittance file, or approving a batch in a bank portal. An AI agent that is shopping freight for a shipper doesn't have hands, a browser session it should be trusted with, or a seat in the accounts payable team. It has HTTP.

articles.title: Everything‑as‑Code is NOT the finish line — my day deleting the ghosts left behind
articles.excerpt: Today I spent a huge chunk of my workday cleaning up leftover junk: old cloud resources, forgotten repos, and Entra ID app registrations nobody remembered existed. Some of this mess came down to rushe…
articles.body: Today I spent a huge chunk of my workday cleaning up leftover junk: old cloud resources, forgotten repos, and Entra ID app registrations nobody remembered existed. Some of this mess came down to rushed, lazy planning. Some was from teammates who’d moved on and never tidied up their work before they left. Sitting there deleting it all, I found myself thinking — isn’t this exactly what everything‑as‑Code is supposed to fix? Turns out: no. IaC is fantastic, but it only manages the resources you remembered to put INTO your IaC repo. If someone quickly clicks together a test Entra ID app registration, spins up a temporary demo environment, or builds a quick prototype outside the repo — those things become invisible ghosts your pipelines will happily ignore.

articles.title: Your AI agent shouldn't see your API keys
articles.excerpt: Three incidents from the past month made me rethink where my agents keep secrets. Cursor. Coding-agent traces stolen in a breach contained users' credentials. The attacker used them to reach other ser…
articles.body: Three incidents from the past month made me rethink where my agents keep secrets. Cursor. Coding-agent traces stolen in a breach contained users' credentials. The attacker used them to reach other services. Phala, a provider behind OpenRouter. The attacker could see request contents, and tokens from those requests were later misused. LLM routers. A recent study tested 428 third-party routers. Nine of them swapped the model's tool calls for malicious ones. Anthropic and OpenAI probably have some of the best security in the world. Smaller providers can be breached, and then a malicious tool call runs on your machine. Where keys usually live Usually keys sit where the agent can reach them. In Hermes, for example, they are stored on disk next to the token for remote server access.

articles.title: I gave 3 image compressors a hard 100KB limit. Only one hit it automatically.
articles.excerpt: Most "image compressor" benchmarks ask the wrong question: which tool makes the smallest file? But a lot of real jobs have a hard cap, not a "smaller is better" goal. A CMS field that rejects anything…
articles.body: Most "image compressor" benchmarks ask the wrong question: which tool makes the smallest file? But a lot of real jobs have a hard cap , not a "smaller is better" goal. A CMS field that rejects anything over 100KB. An email banner. A form attachment limit. For those, the question is: which tool can actually land under my limit, and what does it cost in quality? So I ran that exact task on three tools — same inputs, same 100KB target — and measured exact output bytes plus SSIM. The setup Four synthetic source images (a noisy photo, a gradient photo, a UI screenshot, a noisy graphic), all over 100KB. Target: ≤102,400 bytes (100 KiB) , judged on exact downloaded bytes, not the rounded number each tool shows.

articles.title: Would your chatbot send you to the emergency room for this headache?
articles.excerpt: Two volunteers in an Oxford study, published in Nature Medicine in February 2026, acted out the same case written by doctors: a bleed on the brain, a rare type of stroke. Both typed a terrible headach…
articles.body: Two volunteers in an Oxford study, published in Nature Medicine in February 2026, acted out the same case written by doctors: a bleed on the brain, a rare type of stroke. Both typed a terrible headache, a stiff neck and light that hurt their eyes into GPT-4o. One was told it might be a migraine and to rest in a dark, quiet room. The other also said the headache came on suddenly and was told to go to the emergency room. Across 1,298 UK participants, the chatbots reading the full case alone named the right condition about 95% of the time. People typing to the same chatbots got there in fewer than 34.5% of cases, and the group without a chatbot, mostly using web search or what they already knew, did better at naming it. The AI mostly knew.

articles.body: You have an app idea, a budget that does not look like an Australian agency quote, and a studio in Seoul that says five days. The first thing that usually stops the project is not code. It is the question your accountant asks: "Will there be GST on this invoice?" Here is the order we recommend to Australian founders, and why it saves a week. GST and the overseas supplier A company in Seoul is not registered for Australian GST, so it cannot charge GST on its invoice. If you are registered for GST and you buy services from an offshore supplier, you generally account for the GST yourself on your business activity statement under the reverse-charge rules for inbound intangible supplies.

Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. articles.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
articles.excerpt: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send message…
articles.body: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment.

articles.title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
articles.excerpt: The legend of the Black Knight satellite offers an example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can accumulate into a single conspiracy theory over time.
articles.body: In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction.

articles.title: Dream Chaser space plane gets landing approval for debut mission in 2027
articles.excerpt: Sierra Space's Dream Chaser is aiming for its first spaceflight after more than 20 years of development, and the space plane now has FAA approval to come home.
articles.body: The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut. Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. "Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9). The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated .
